topics.title: Review of Fiqh and Iman (JSS2)
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the five pillars of Islam.
The students should be able to explain the six articles of faith.
The students should be able to differentiate between Fiqh and Iman.

Introduction:
Today we will review what we learned about Fiqh and Iman in JSS2. This review will help us build a strong foundation for our Islamic studies this term.

Content:
Arkan al-Islam refers to the five pillars of Islam which are the foundation of a Muslim's practice. These pillars are: Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salat (prayer), Zakat (charity), Sawm (fasting during Ramadan), and Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca). In Nigeria, we see these pillars in daily life - from the call to prayer in our neighborhoods to the Zakat given during Eid celebrations.

Arkan al-Iman refers to the six articles of faith which are the beliefs that must be held by a Muslim. These are: belief in Allah, belief in His angels, belief in His books, belief in His messengers, belief in the Day of Judgment, and belief in divine destiny. These articles form the core of our faith and guide how we understand the world around us.

Fiqh is the understanding and application of Islamic laws and practices in daily life. It deals with the practical aspects of worship and transactions. Iman, on the other hand, is the faith and belief in the heart. While Fiqh is about actions, Iman is about the conviction in the heart. A good example is that knowing how to perform ablution (Wudu) is Fiqh, while believing that Allah commands Wudu is part of Iman.

Class activity:
Divide the class into two groups. One group will list the five pillars of Islam with examples from Nigerian context. The other group will list the six articles of faith with brief explanations. Each group will present their findings to the class.

Evaluation questions:
1. List the five pillars of Islam.
2. What are the six articles of faith?
3. How is Fiqh different from Iman?
4. Give an example of how a pillar of Islam is practiced in Nigeria.

Summary:
Today we reviewed the fundamental aspects of Islam and faith that we learned in JSS2, which will help us understand more complex topics in Islamic Studies this term.

topics.title: Funeral Rites in Islam
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to describe the process of washing (Ghusl) a deceased Muslim.
The students should be able to list the steps for shrouding the body (Kafan).
The students should be able to explain the funeral prayer (Janazah) and burial procedures.

Introduction:
In Islam, death is seen as a natural transition from this life to the hereafter. Today we will learn about the proper Islamic funeral rites as taught by our Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).

Content:
When a Muslim dies, the body must be washed (Ghusl) as soon as possible, preferably by the same gender. The washing process involves: laying the body on a flat surface, covering the private parts, starting with the right side, using clean water and soap if available, and reciting verses from the Quran. In Nigeria, families often perform this ritual at home or in the mosque with the help of knowledgeable community members.

After washing, the body is shrouded (Kafan) in simple white cloth, preferably made of cotton. For males, there are three pieces: the lower garment (izar), the upper garment (rida), and the head cover. For females, there are five pieces including the head cover and the chest wrapper. This simple shrouding reminds us that in death, all people are equal regardless of their wealth or status in society.

The funeral prayer (Janazah) is performed with the body present, facing the qiblah (Mecca). It consists of Takbir (Allahu Akbar) four times, with supplications in between. The Janazah can be performed in a mosque, prayer ground, or even in a field if necessary. In Nigeria, communities often gather to perform this prayer together, showing unity and support for the grieving family.

Burial should take place as soon as possible, preferably on the same day if possible. The grave should be oriented so the body faces Mecca. The body is placed on its right side, facing the qiblah. Simple gravestones are permitted, but elaborate structures are discouraged. This reflects Islamic values of simplicity and focus on the afterlife rather than worldly displays.

Class activity:
Role-play the funeral rites process in groups. One group will demonstrate the washing process, another will show the shrouding, and a third will lead the class in performing the Janazah prayer. After each demonstration, discuss the key points.

Evaluation questions:
1. Describe the steps for washing a deceased Muslim.
2. How many pieces are used for shrouding a male and a female body?
3. What are the key components of the Janazah prayer?
4. Why is prompt burial important in Islam?
5. How do Islamic funeral rites reflect the values of equality and simplicity?

Summary:
Islamic funeral rites provide clear guidelines for treating the deceased with dignity and respect, while comforting the living with the promise of Allah's mercy and the hope of reunion in the hereafter.

topics.title: Marriage in Islam
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the conditions of a valid marriage in Islam.
The students should be able to list the types of marriage recognized in Islam.
The students should be able to explain the rights and responsibilities of spouses in Islam.

Introduction:
Marriage is a sacred institution in Islam that establishes the family unit as the foundation of society. Today we will explore the Islamic perspective on marriage, its conditions, types, and the mutual rights and responsibilities between husband and wife.

Content:
For a marriage to be valid in Islam, certain conditions must be met. First, both parties must consent freely without any coercion. In Nigeria, we see this in how families negotiate marriages but ultimately respect the wishes of the couple. Second, there must be at least two witnesses to the marriage contract. Third, the marriage must be announced publicly to prevent secret relationships. Fourth, the dowry (Mahr) must be specified, which is a gift from the husband to the wife. This can be money, property, or other valuable items, and in Nigerian culture, it often includes practical items like a sewing machine or furniture for the new home.

Islam recognizes different types of marriage. The most common is the permanent marriage (Nikah), which is intended to be lifelong. Another type is the fixed-term marriage (Mut'ah), which is practiced by some Muslim communities but is not widely accepted in Nigeria. Islam also discourages forced marriages, emphasizing that both parties must enter the marriage willingly and with full understanding of their commitment.

In Islam, marriage is based on mutual rights and responsibilities. The husband has the responsibility to provide for the family's financial needs, including food, clothing, and shelter. He must also treat his wife with kindness and respect. The wife has the right to be maintained by her husband and to be treated with dignity. She also has responsibilities to care for the home and children, and to be faithful and obedient to her husband in matters that do not contradict Islam. In Nigerian families, we see these principles in how husbands work to provide for their families while wives manage the household and children's upbringing.

Class activity:
Divide the class into small groups. Each group will create a role-play demonstrating a scenario showing how a husband and wife fulfill their rights and responsibilities in a typical Nigerian Muslim family situation. Each group will perform their role-play for the class.

Evaluation questions:
1. What are the four conditions for a valid marriage in Islam?
2. Name two types of marriage recognized in Islam.
3. What is the purpose of the dowry (Mahr) in Islamic marriage?
4. Explain the husband's financial responsibility in marriage.
5. How does Islam ensure balance of rights between husband and wife?

Summary:
Islamic marriage provides a comprehensive framework that balances the rights and responsibilities of spouses, creating a stable and loving family environment based on mutual respect and shared values.

topics.title: Inheritance (Mirath)
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the basic principles of inheritance in Islam.
The students should be able to identify the main categories of heirs in Islam.
The students should be able to calculate simple inheritance shares using basic examples.

Introduction:
Islam provides a detailed system of inheritance that ensures fair distribution of wealth among heirs after a person's death. Today we will learn about these principles and how they work in practice.

Content:
The basic principles of inheritance in Islam are derived from the Quran and the Sunnah of Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). First, inheritance distribution is a religious obligation that must be carried out. Second, only relatives who are named as heirs in Islamic law inherit; others do not. Third, debts must be paid from the estate before distribution. Fourth, shares are determined by Allah and cannot be changed by human will. In Nigeria, these principles are followed in Islamic courts and by families who wish to adhere to Islamic inheritance laws.

Islam recognizes different categories of heirs. The primary heirs include spouses, children, parents, and siblings. Secondary heirs include grandparents, uncles, aunts, and cousins. The Quran specifies fixed shares for some heirs, while others inherit as residuary. For example, the wife receives one-fourth of the estate if there are no children, and one-eighth if there are children. The son receives twice the share of the daughter. In Nigerian families, this system ensures that wealth is distributed according to clear Islamic guidelines rather than according to personal preferences or favoritism.

The process of calculating inheritance involves several steps. First, determine all debts and funeral expenses that must be paid from the estate. Second, identify all heirs and their relationship to the deceased. Third, apply the fixed shares as specified in the Quran. Fourth, distribute any remaining estate among the residuary heirs. For example, if a man dies leaving behind a wife, two daughters, and a son, the wife gets one-eighth, each daughter gets one-sixth, and the son gets one-third. This example shows how shares are calculated and distributed according to Islamic principles.

Class activity:
Provide students with simple inheritance scenarios to solve in groups. For example: "If a man dies leaving behind a wife, two sons, and three daughters, how would his estate be divided according to Islamic inheritance law?" Groups will work together to calculate the shares and present their solutions to the class.

Evaluation questions:
1. What are the four basic principles of inheritance in Islam?
2. List three categories of heirs recognized in Islam.
3. What share does a wife inherit if there are no children?
4. How does Islam ensure fairness in inheritance distribution?
5. Why must debts be paid before distributing inheritance?

Summary:
The Islamic system of inheritance provides clear guidelines for fair distribution of wealth that balances the needs of different family members while maintaining social justice and family cohesion.

topics.title: MID-TERM EXAMINATION
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate their understanding of Islamic laws and practices covered this term.
The students should be able to apply knowledge of funeral rites, marriage, and inheritance to practical situations.

Introduction:
Today is your mid-term examination. This test will assess your understanding of the Islamic laws and practices we have covered this term, including funeral rites, marriage, and inheritance.

Content:
The examination will cover the following topics:

1. Review of Fiqh and Iman (JSS2)
 - The five pillars of Islam
 - The six articles of faith
 - Difference between Fiqh and Iman

2. Funeral Rites in Islam
 - Washing (Ghusl) of the deceased
 - Shrouding (Kafan) procedures
 - Funeral prayer (Janazah)
 - Burial procedures

3. Marriage in Islam
 - Conditions of valid marriage
 - Types of marriage
 - Rights and responsibilities of spouses
 - Dowry (Mahr)

4. Inheritance (Mirath)
 - Basic principles of inheritance
 - Categories of heirs
 - Calculation of inheritance shares

The examination will consist of multiple-choice questions, short answer questions, and one scenario-based question that requires you to apply your knowledge to a practical situation.

Class activity:
Students will complete the examination under examination conditions. They should work independently and follow all examination rules.

Evaluation questions:
The examination questions will test your knowledge and understanding of the topics covered this term.

Summary:
Complete your examination carefully and to the best of your ability. Your results will help identify areas where you may need additional study before continuing with the remaining topics this term.

topics.title: Faith in Allah and His Attributes
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list the beautiful names of Allah.
The students should be able to explain the importance of Tawhid in Islam.
The students should be able to differentiate between the attributes of Allah and human attributes.

Introduction:
Our faith in Islam begins with belief in Allah, the Creator and Sustainer of all that exists. Today we will explore the concept of Tawhid and understand the beautiful names and attributes of Allah as described in the Quran and Sunnah.

Content:
Allah has ninety-nine beautiful names (Al-Asma al-Husna) that describe His perfect attributes. These names include Ar-Rahman (The Most Gracious), Ar-Rahim (The Most Merciful), Al-Malik (The King), Al-Quddus (The Most Holy), As-Salam (The Source of Peace), Al-Mu'min (The Giver of Faith), Al-Muhaymin (The Protector), Al-'Aziz (The Mighty), Al-Jabbar (The Compeller), and Al-Mutakabbir (The Supreme). Each name reveals an aspect of Allah's nature and helps us understand His relationship with creation. In Nigerian Muslim communities, these names are often recited in daily prayers and remembrance (Dhikr) to strengthen faith.

Tawhid is the concept of the oneness and uniqueness of Allah. It is the foundation of Islamic faith and the most important principle in Islam. Tawhid means recognizing that Allah is one, without partners, equals, or rivals. This belief affects every aspect of a Muslim's life, from worship to daily conduct. In Nigeria, we see Tawhid demonstrated in the declaration of faith (Shahadah) that Muslims recite daily: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the messenger of Allah." This simple declaration encapsulates the core of Islamic belief.

The attributes of Allah are perfect and cannot be compared to human attributes. For example, when we say Allah is "All-Hearing" (As-Sami'), it does not mean He has ears like humans. Rather, it means He has perfect hearing that encompasses all things without limitation. Similarly, when we say Allah is "All-Knowing" (Al-'Alim), it does not mean He learns like humans; rather, His knowledge encompasses all things, past, present, and future. Understanding this distinction is crucial to maintaining proper belief and avoiding anthropomorphism (attributing human characteristics to Allah).

Class activity:
Divide the class into groups. Each group will select five of Allah's names, explain their meanings, and provide examples of how understanding these names can help Muslims in their daily lives in Nigeria. Each group will present their findings to the class.

Evaluation questions:
1. List any five of Allah's beautiful names and explain their meanings.
2. What is Tawhid and why is it important in Islam?
3. How are Allah's attributes different from human attributes?
4. Give an example of how belief in Allah's attributes affects a Muslim's daily life.
5. Why is it important to understand Allah's names correctly?

Summary:
Understanding Allah's beautiful names and attributes, and the concept of Tawhid, strengthens our faith and guides us in living a life that pleases our Creator.

topics.title: MID-TERM BREAK
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to relax and recharge for the second half of the term.
The students should be able to reflect on what they have learned so far this term.

Introduction:
Today marks the beginning of our mid-term break. This is a time for rest, relaxation, and reflection on the knowledge you have gained in Islamic Studies so far this term.

Content:
During this break, you should take time to rest your mind and body. The mid-term break is an opportunity to recharge your energy so that you can return to school ready to learn new concepts with fresh minds. You may also use this time to revise what we have covered this term, including the review of Fiqh and Iman, funeral rites, marriage in Islam, inheritance, and faith in Allah and His attributes.

Reflection is an important part of the learning process. During the break, consider how the knowledge you have gained in Islamic Studies can be applied to your daily life. Think about how understanding Islamic funeral rites helps you appreciate the value of life and the importance of preparing for the hereafter. Reflect on how the Islamic principles of marriage and inheritance promote justice and family harmony in society.

Class activity:
No formal class activity during the break. However, students are encouraged to engage in beneficial activities that strengthen their faith and knowledge, such as reading the Quran, learning more about the life of Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), or spending time with family discussing Islamic values.

Evaluation questions:
No formal evaluation during the break.

Summary:
Enjoy your mid-term break, use this time to rest and reflect on what you have learned, and return to school prepared to continue your Islamic studies with renewed energy and focus.

topics.title: Belief in the Holy Books
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the names of the holy books mentioned in Islam, explain the role of revelation in human life, and differentiate between the Qur'an and previous revelations.

Introduction:
Today we will learn about the belief in holy books in Islam. We have previously discussed the concept of Tawhid, which is the oneness of Allah, and now we will explore how Allah guides humanity through His revelations.

Content:
The Holy Books in Islam are revelations from Allah to His prophets. The main holy books include the Tawrah (Torah) revealed to Prophet Musa (Moses), the Zabur (Psalms) revealed to Prophet Dawud (David), the Injil (Gospel) revealed to Prophet Isa (Jesus), and the Qur'an revealed to Prophet Muhammad (SAW). The Qur'an is the final and complete revelation that confirms and supersedes all previous revelations. Revelation plays a crucial role in human life as it provides guidance, moral values, and laws to live a righteous life. In Nigeria, we can see how the teachings of the Qur'an influence our daily activities, from how we conduct business at the market to how we treat our neighbors. The Qur'an was revealed over 23 years and has been preserved in its original form since then, unlike previous revelations which were altered by human beings over time.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups of four to create a chart comparing the four main holy books, including the prophet each was revealed to, its main message, and its status in Islam today.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name three holy books mentioned in Islam besides the Qur'an.
2. Explain why the Qur'an is considered the final revelation.
3. How does revelation guide human life according to Islamic teachings?
4. What is the difference between the Qur'an and previous revelations in terms of preservation?

Summary:
Belief in holy books is a fundamental aspect of Islamic faith, with the Qur'an being the final and complete guidance for humanity.

topics.title: Belief in the Hereafter
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the concept of accountability in Islam, describe the characteristics of Paradise and Hellfire, and identify how belief in the Hereafter affects a Muslim's daily life.

Introduction:
We have learned about Allah's guidance through His revelations, and today we will explore what happens after death in Islamic belief. This connects to our previous discussions about Allah's justice and mercy.

Content:
Belief in the Hereafter (Akhirah) is one of the six articles of faith in Islam. Muslims believe that life in this world is temporary and that there will be a day of judgment when every person will be held accountable for their deeds. The accountability will be based on one's faith and good actions. Paradise (Jannah) is the eternal reward for the righteous, described as a place with rivers flowing beneath, abundant fruits, and companions who are pure. Hellfire (Jahannam) is the punishment for the disbelievers and sinners, characterized by intense heat, fire, and severe torment. In Nigeria, during the Harmattan season, we experience some discomfort from the cold and dust, but the punishment in Hellfire is far greater and eternal. The Qur'an describes the details of both Paradise and Hellfire to motivate Muslims to live righteously.

Class activity:
Students will write a short paragraph explaining how belief in the Hereafter affects their daily decisions, such as honesty in exams, treatment of others, and prayer.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the Islamic concept of accountability after death?
2. Describe two characteristics of Paradise mentioned in the Qur'an.
3. How does belief in the Hereafter influence a Muslim's behavior?
4. What is the difference between the temporary trials of this life and the eternal nature of the Hereafter?

Summary:
Belief in the Hereafter reminds Muslims that this life is a test and that their actions will have eternal consequences.

topics.title: Living a Life of Faith
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify ways to apply Iman in daily actions, explain the relationship between faith and good deeds, and list practical examples of living a life of faith in a Nigerian context.

Introduction:
After learning about the articles of faith, including belief in Allah, His prophets, books, angels, the Hereafter, and predestination, today we will focus on how to put these beliefs into practice in our daily lives.

Content:
Living a life of faith (Iman) means that our beliefs guide our actions. In Islam, faith without good deeds is incomplete. The Qur'an states that people are only judged by their intentions and actions. A Muslim should demonstrate their faith through the Five Pillars of Islam: Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (prayer), Zakat (charity), Sawm (fasting), and Hajj (pilgrimage). Beyond these pillars, faith is shown in honesty, kindness, and justice in all dealings. In Nigeria, this means being fair when buying and selling at the market, helping neighbors in need, and maintaining good character even when facing difficulties like traffic in Lagos or challenges during the farming season. The Prophet Muhammad (SAW) said that the best among Muslims are those with the best character. Living a life of faith also means following the teachings of Islam in modern situations, such as using technology responsibly and maintaining modesty in appearance.

Class activity:
Students will create a "Faith in Action" journal for one week, recording how they demonstrated their faith through good deeds, words, and thoughts each day.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the relationship between faith and good deeds in Islam?
2. Give two examples of how a student can show faith at school.
3. How does belief in Allah affect a Muslim's business practices in Nigeria?
4. Why is good character considered an important aspect of living a life of faith?

Summary:
Living a life of faith requires Muslims to embody their beliefs through righteous actions and good character in all aspects of life.

topics.title: REVISION
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall the main concepts studied in Fiqh and Iman, explain the relationship between different topics covered, and apply Islamic teachings to practical situations.

Introduction:
We have covered many important topics this term, and today we will review what we have learned about Fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence) and Iman (faith) to prepare for our end-of-term examination.

Content:
Our revision will focus on the key areas we studied this term. For Fiqh, we reviewed the purification process (Taharah), including Wudu (ablution) and Ghusl (ritual bath), and Salah (prayer) with its conditions and different types. We also studied Zakat (obligatory charity), its calculation, and recipients. For Iman, we covered the six articles of faith: belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His prophets, the Hereafter, and divine decree. We also discussed belief in the Holy Books and the Hereafter in detail. It is important to understand how these concepts connect. For example, belief in Allah leads us to perform Salah, belief in the Hereafter motivates us to give Zakat, and belief in divine decree helps us accept life's challenges with patience. In Nigerian contexts, these teachings apply to our daily interactions, business practices, and community service.

Class activity:
Students will participate in a group quiz competition where teams take turns answering questions about Fiqh and Iman topics covered this term.

Evaluation questions:
1. List the six articles of faith in Islam.
2. Explain the process of performing Wudu according to Islamic teachings.
3. How does belief in the Hereafter affect a Muslim's generosity?
4. What are the conditions for valid Salah?
5. Give an example of how Islamic teachings can be applied in a Nigerian market setting.

Summary:
Understanding and applying the teachings of Fiqh and Iman is essential for living as a faithful Muslim in all aspects of life.

topics.title: EXAMINATION
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate their understanding of Islamic Studies concepts through written examination, apply Islamic teachings to various scenarios, and reflect on their learning this term.

Introduction:
Today is your end-of-term examination in Islamic Studies. This assessment will test your knowledge and understanding of the topics we have covered this term, including Belief in the Holy Books, Belief in the Hereafter, and Living a Life of Faith.

Content:
The examination will consist of multiple-choice questions, short-answer questions, and essay questions covering all topics studied this term. You will need to demonstrate your knowledge of the six articles of faith, the Five Pillars of Islam, and specific details about the Holy Books and the Hereafter. You should also be prepared to apply Islamic teachings to practical situations, such as how to handle peer pressure, conduct business honestly, or show kindness to others. Remember that this examination is not just about testing your memory but also about understanding how to live as a Muslim in contemporary Nigerian society. Your answers should reflect both knowledge and application of Islamic principles.

Class activity:
Students will complete the written examination under supervised conditions.

Evaluation questions:
The examination will serve as the evaluation, with questions covering all topics studied this term.

Summary:
This examination allows you to demonstrate your understanding of Islamic teachings and how they apply to your daily life as a Muslim student in Nigeria.

topics.title: CLOSING/VACATION
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to reflect on their learning this term, identify areas for improvement in their Islamic practice, and set goals for their religious studies during the vacation.

Introduction:
As we conclude this term of Islamic Studies, it is important to reflect on what we have learned and how we can continue growing in our faith during the vacation period.

Content:
Today marks the end of the third term in Islamic Studies. We have covered important topics including Belief in the Holy Books, Belief in the Hereafter, and Living a Life of Faith. As you go on vacation, remember that learning about Islam is a continuous process. Use this time to strengthen your relationship with Allah through increased prayer, reading the Qur'an, and performing good deeds. In Nigeria, vacation is also a time when families come together, so use these opportunities to share what you have learned with younger siblings and relatives. Set specific goals for yourself during the break, such as memorizing additional verses of the Qur'an, learning more about the life of Prophet Muhammad (SAW), or participating in community service. Remember that the vacation is also a time to rest and recharge for the upcoming term.

Class activity:
Students will write a personal reflection on one concept they learned this term that they find most meaningful and how they plan to implement it in their life during the vacation.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is one important concept you learned in Islamic Studies this term?
2. How will you continue your Islamic studies during the vacation?
3. Name one good deed you plan to do during the vacation.
4. How will you share your knowledge of Islam with family members during the break?

Summary:
As you enjoy your vacation, remember to maintain and strengthen your Islamic practice and continue seeking knowledge about your faith.
